sm: This is the Williamson County winter basketball media day, with wrestling also running in a back room. The first team is Centennial. Boys coach Sloan Starkey, in his second year, says the team graduated five players and returns one starter. He praises sophomore forward Miles Elam, seniors Luke Henrick and Burke Keaton, junior Ethan Mungy and Logan Williamson, and expects Keaton to average at least twenty points. Girls coach Shane Chapman, in his first year, thanks veterans, says about fifteen to eighteen girls are out, three players return, and eight graduated. He introduces his daughter Mercy, a six-foot sophomore, plus Charlie Yingling and Erin Gilbert.

The Centennial girls coach adds that his squad has several new upperclassmen and about six freshmen, and that tryouts began October twenty-sixth. Asked about coaching his daughter Mercy, he says he asks whether she is speaking to Dad or to Coach, and that she acts as a liaison to teammates. Mercy says it has been fun and that he pushes her hard. He admits last year's team had the highest turnover rate of his twenty-five years and shot poorly. This year the focus is fundamentals: off-hand dribbling, fake passes, screens, and good passes leading to easy looks.

The Centennial girls coach says he recruits in the hallways and sells efficient, scheduled practices, and the older girls are mentoring freshmen. Burke Keaton says his coach is pushing him to be a better leader. Coach Starkey says last year's up-and-down results came with a first-year coach and new system, and this group has done more voluntary offseason work. Mercy says she feels some pressure as an all-district returner and sees the team changing the girls program's trend. Next is Brentwood, with girls coach Eddie Walker, first year, and Callie Whitfield, and boys coach Troy Crane, third year, with Auburn signee Davis Cochrane. Crane says the word for his team is retooling after losing a three-year point guard and a shooter.

Coach Crane describes his roster by class, naming seniors Luke Matthew and Parker Emerson, juniors Miles Timms, Jake West, Parker Platt and Ezra Nieves, and transfer Graham Serifen. Parker Platt is six-eight and also plays volleyball. Crane says no one has had full participation since spring practice because many play multiple sports. Girls coach Eddie Walker says his group has a great work ethic and attitude, with two seniors and big junior and freshman classes. Next week they play a tough schedule at Smyrna, Upperman and Lebanon. Crane calls Jake West the glue guy and expects Luke Matthew to score a lot. Davis Cochrane says committing before the season took weight off his shoulders.

Davis Cochrane says he will lean on family, coaches and teammates to block out outside noise after signing with Auburn. Brentwood's girls coach credits team culture and bringing two separate units together. Callie Whitfield says last year pressure took away the fun, and this year they are enjoying the game again. Coach Crane says the team has three players over six-seven, so rebounding is a strength, and Davis moves to a guard role on offense with Parker Platt and Jake West protecting the rim. Davis says he feels less limited and can show his versatility. Callie's favorite games are district games. Davis hopes to face Bartlett, the top-ranked team in the country that eliminated them last year.

Davis Cochrane says he believes he can compete with anyone in the country and wants another shot at Bartlett. Next up are the Franklin Admirals. Interim girls coach Simone Newman, in her seventh year in the county, and boys coach Jason Tiger, in his eighth season, give opening statements. Tiger says the team graduated a lot and he loves developing chemistry in preseason. Players Ali King and Colin Robinson both say last year's team could not finish games and plans to compete all four quarters with a next-play mentality. Tiger praises Colin's growth as a leader. Ali says the move from Coach Shaw, who stepped away for family reasons, has not been a big adjustment.

Coach Newman says the all-women coaching staff has been consistent, so the leadership change feels no different. Coach Tiger, the longest-tenured boys coach in 4A, recalls painful losses, including a COVID-year sub-state loss at Clarksville, a region semifinal against Independence, and a loss to Centennial after beating them three times. He says this team is hungry, with four starters graduated and others who waited their turn. Colin Robinson, a returning all-region player, says he has a chip on his shoulder in his senior season. Ali King says last year's offense relied on the post, so they will be a shorter, shooting team, adding post Clara from Ravenwood. Both coaches say the one-time transfer rule will not change how they coach, though Tiger will keep more freshmen. Next is Nolensville.

The Nolensville Knights are represented by girls coach Chris Lad, in his eleventh year, with Addie Harris, and boys coach Drew Gaddice, in his fifth year, with Tucker Powers. Lad says three starters return, five seniors must be replaced, and he hopes to compete for district and region titles, with newcomers such as Kendall Jepsen, Scarlett Spain and Taelyn Musquita. Gaddice says the boys return less than fifteen percent of production and are far from a finished product, but he is thinking about February. Players say the girls have great chemistry and want to reach state, and the boys have high potential and are familiar with each other. They are asked what makes Nolensville special.

Players and coaches describe Nolensville as a close, supportive community with a small-town feel, where coaches attend each other's games. Coaches say the extra week of practice brought adjustments. One said practice twelve on Monday was terrible, while another said the team scrimmaged and gave up twenty-nine in a first quarter, showing defensive buy-in still needs work. A player is most looking forward to playing Ravenwood. Both coaches say the one-time transfer rule cuts both ways, they have benefited and been hurt, and they will coach the kids in front of them, preferring players who are fully committed. Next are the Independence Eagles: girls coach Jeremy Whaley, first year, with MJ Montgomery, and boys coach Jeremy Moore, back for a second stint, with Kobe Jackson.

Coach Whaley is glad to coach girls he watched from afar and notes MJ Montgomery signed that day. Coach Moore says the buy-in began with his best player, and he wants to build a base of guarding and rebounding. He returned partly because of Independence's strong players and administration, and says Kobe Jackson, who scored seventeen against him as a sophomore, is a competitive, strong, well-rounded player who signed with Johnson University. MJ says the seniors are leading a player-led team. Whaley says six seniors, including two who returned after sitting out, make the transition easier. MJ says she already trusted Whaley because he was around practice before.

Kobe Jackson says Independence has a target on its back, but players who stepped up will produce. MJ Montgomery says she knows who she is despite the pressure of her family's name on the school wall. Coach Whaley says his style is high energy and the girls have shown up ready to work, and the biggest difference between coaching boys and girls is that girls are very literal. Coach Moore says the first district game is February second, with eighteen games before it, a three-week district season and no district tournament. He and another coach prefer no district tournament, since they dislike playing the same teams repeatedly, though a short district stretch makes injuries costly.

Players say Paige is the team Independence most wants to face. Next are the Ravenwood Raptors. Girls coach Dallas Mall, in his first year, praises senior shooting guard Cora Havilland as the voice of the locker room, on a young team with nine sophomores. Boys coach Chris Hooper, in his second year, says last year's nineteen and twelve team reached sub-state and lost seven seniors. He praises seniors Thomas Broden, Braden White, Graham Higginbotham and Chase Roberts, and says the team will play faster, up and down the floor and shoot more threes. Cora says sharing a vision with Coach Mall has made practices run smoothly and the girls more bought in.

Ravenwood players say they are hungry after last year's sub-state loss and that culture matters most. Coach Hooper says the biggest challenge is complacency with young players and he stresses getting one percent better each day. Coach Mall says moving up from middle school was not a big adjustment because core principles translate. Hooper says the extra practice week has been refreshing, and he is being strategic with days off. A player says the extra practice is tiring but helps. Ravenwood opens on Tuesday against Warren County. On the one-time transfer rule, Coach Mall says coaches must be strategic, such as considering whether to keep a freshman on varsity.

Coach Mall says he focuses on developing players and wants kids who want to be at Ravenwood. Players name Brentwood, the Battle of the Woods, and Paige as games they look forward to. Mall describes six-three freshman Austin Strange as a big inside presence still learning. Next are the Paige Patriots. Girls coach Randy Kauffman, in his fifth year, says the team returns experience after reaching the state tournament, and his player Jordan Maddox signs with Cumberland University. Boys coach Jared Street, in his sixth year, says the team went eighteen and nine, returns eight of its top ten, and has one of his hardest schedules. Owen Looney will sign with Freed-Hardeman.

Coach Kauffman says being the team others want to beat is a compliment, and Paige plays over half its schedule at exposure events across the southeast. Players say the team is close, works hard, and puts in extra time in the gym. Coach Street says the boys chose tough games over winning percentage, with a California team, Huntsville, Alabama, a Mobile team, Brentwood Academy, and the Battle for Nashville. A player says last year's early-round loss motivates them. A reporter asks who sets the high bar, and coaches credit athletic director Benji Gray and the administration. Kauffman says the girls team has a weighted grade point average of four point two six. Coaches say they value support for both academics and athletics.

Paige coaches say a tough schedule teaches teams to stay balanced and be comfortable with hard things, with the goal of being tough and together by the end of February. Players say basketball stands apart because of its conditioning and many skills. Asked which Williamson County school they would most like to beat, one player says Nolensville after a loss last year. Owen Looney says his twin brothers on the team each help. Coaches say the extra practice week reduced rushing, helped with agility and weight room work, and allowed days off, with scripted practices reaching roughly eighty to ninety-three minutes of a one-hundred-fifteen-minute plan. Players say it helped them teach younger teammates and learn from scrimmage mistakes.

Paige players say scrimmages and practices show flaws to fix before February and March. Next are the Summit Spartans. Girls coach Donald George, in his third year, has many returning and younger girls, and boys coach Thad Burgess, in his fourth year, says his team is starting from scratch in some ways. Coach George says leaders like Sam Malcolm, Trinity Garcia and Caroline French have stepped up, and young girls bring energy. Players say opponents should not count Summit out, as the team works hard and is close. Asked about the four-team district, coaches say it is out of their control and the region is tough. One notes scheduling can be harder, but they plan some games with Rutherford County teams.

Coach George says the freshman class is high energy, naming Riley Maines, Brooklyn Sale, Madeleine McElhaney and Eliza Fox, and he opens the gym at five forty-five in the morning. Coach Burgess says the school has about seventeen hundred students, and Drew Soph went from junior varsity starter to varsity leader. Both coaches say the extra practice week helps young teams, and boys scrimmaged the night before. Players say they want to play. On the one-time transfer rule, Burgess says it has not affected him yet and he wants players who want to be there. Players look forward to playing Independence and visiting CPA's new gym.

Summit players say the Indy game is always the best atmosphere, and Coach Burgess says the short district schedule means moved dates and Thursday games, but kids adapt. He likes the nostalgia of district tournaments but dislikes playing the same opponents back to back. Next are the Fairview Yellow Jackets. Girls coach Isaac Edmondson, in his second year, has nearly everyone back and no seniors, and says they won as many games this summer as all last season. Boys coach Trey McCoy, in his tenth season, the longest-tenured county boys coach, says the team is young, athletic and has experience from last year. He says the girls learned to take care of the ball and not fold.

Players say Fairview never gives up even when down by twenty. Coach McCoy discusses his assistant coach, a former player, and describes a six-seven center who protects guards, plus senior Aemon Birch, who has dealt with injuries, and sophomore Giles Brown, an elite finisher. Coach Edmondson names Lila Varden, Cassidy Walker, Bella Anderson, newcomer Sofia Butchery, and freshmen Mikayla Brewer and Adley. He says the girls have six-footers this year. Lila says the returning players can teach younger girls, giving more time to grow together.

Fairview players say the boys have long-standing chemistry, and McCoy says young kids grew up together and the team welcomes newcomers. The community support includes a longtime bookkeeper and fans who never miss events. Players say the football team's eleven and zero record raises standards and excitement. Coaches say they would like a longer preseason than the extra week, and players say it helped their young teams and scrimmages. On transfers, the coaches say Fairview mostly gets families who relocate, not transfers, and they coach whoever wants to be there. As the only 3A county school, players look forward to facing Marshall County, Houston County and Centennial. The host then closes the 2026 media day.
